
You've demonstrated that a crate can solve it *without* the compiler, too.
So why does it need to be in the compiler?

If the aim is to automatically apply this transform (something only the compiler can do), then:
- [the drop order changes](https://github.com/yaspar-org/yaspar-macros/blob/main/README.md#limitations) are a blocker
- automatically transforming unsafe code could cause unsoundness
- adding to heap usage might not be desirable (or possible, as Vorpal said)
- performance could be impacted

If the aim is to add an attribute/macro to the compiler (or the standard library), then the bar is high. The feature needs to do things that can only be done in the compiler / standard library, or extend standard library types (or traits/lang items, in this case). Otherwise "just use the crate" will be the answer.

But all those decisions might not need to be made yet.

If you're looking at the compiler, then the process would be a lang experiment:
https://lang-team.rust-lang.org/how_to/experiment.html

For the standard library, the first step is a design iteration discussion: https://std-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/development/feature-lifecycle.html#suitability-for-the-standard-library

There's also a note at the top of that page about focusing on real problems people are encountering. Do you have data on how prevalent stack overflows are in practice in Rust?

@_**Vorpal|743310** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/131828-t-compiler/topic/Drop.20causes.20stack.20overflow.20for.20deeply.20nested.20data.20structures/near/621296831):
```quote
That is an interesting example crate, but the docs immediately talk about the heap. How would this work in no-std (which I presume would be desirable for a compiler based implementation)?
```

Stack frame needs to come from somewhere. If system stack size is fixed, then it needs to come from somewhere else. For no-std, I can only think of two solutions:

1. Define your own allocator or memory management mechanism that can consume all memory physically possible. 
2. Bound your recursion depths as @**Hanna Kruppe** mentioned.

However, I would raise a point that, for many applications, a recursion bound is a simple idea but not necessarily a good solution. The root problem in this discussion is how to resolve a fixed stack size from the ambient environment setup, let it be your OS or your embedded system. Again, it is the stack size that is bound. A limit on the recursion depths is only an abstraction. Each recursion could have a different frame size, and the same recursion depth might or might not cause stack overflow depending on its initial call sites. In practical, blowing up stack with the same data in different call sites might be rare, but not entirely impossible. The right solution should be a peace in mind. The only limitation should be how much memory you have.

If anyone has ideas about how to make no-std work, I am happy to incorporate.

```quote
However, I would raise a point that, for many applications, a recursion bound is a simple idea but not necessarily a good solution.
```

I don't think unlimited size queues or channels is a good idea in general in any serious program. It is too easy to end up in resource exhaustion. This is why you use back pressure in concurrent systems, rather than unlimited queues. The same goes for stack usage. You shouldn't build unlimited recursive data structures in the first place. You have the wrong abstraction. Or you didn't validate the depth of your untrusted input.

By the time you hit stack overflow it is already too late, your design should have prevented it in the first place.

621487798.en:
@**teor** I don't mean it's compiler's sole responsibility. I think I would rephrase it a bit: providing a universal solution to stack overflow requires significant inputs from the compiler. What the crate does at this moment is somewhere in the middle; it is what a proc-macro can do the best for the few iterations I did. 

What I demonstrated in the crate is, that this is purely a program transformation problem. However, in practice, this is more than a **syntactic** transformation problem, due to how much information a proc-macro is exposed to. All the limitations or caveats the crate has can be resolved if the compiler provides that information. For example, to address the drop order issue, the transformation algorithm needs to know the drop order prior to the transformation, and then drop calls can be inserted in that exact order. This information, of course, cannot be obtained at this moment in a proc-macro. Hence this is a compiler limitation.  

I am not saying the compiler should always perform this transformation. This is not the message I am trying to convey. What I am trying to explain here, is that the compiler should (and must) do something to enable a fully generalized, graceful solution to this problem. It is OK to let a separate crate to do the job (and it's OK to not be part of stdlib too), but the compiler so far lacks functionality to resolve this problem.

Coming back to the title, what can I do if the compiler is not helping me to prevent stack overflow from drop calls? Drop calls are largely inserted by the compiler, but the compiler goes hands-off when an automatically generated and inserted function blows up my stack? This doesn't sound right.

You have the wrong abstraction. Or you didn't validate the depth of your untrusted input.


I wouldn't really go this far in a discussion. A universal argument against a deep recursion without considering the actual problem is unfruitful. I am not looking into a problem just because it's there. Drop call stack overflow is a problem many have hit and wonder a solution to. A search on the internet reveals tons on reddit, dated back many years ago. The little support in compiler to resolve this issue is surprising to me. 

Your parallel to concurrency also makes little sense. Job queue implies limited CPU resources, which could lead to problems like starvation; it's a resource management problem. But recursion has nothing to do with resources. It is a mathematically graceful style to organize programs, nothing more and nothing less. It ought to be a choice, if the ambient system permits. Stack overflow is just a side product, a limitation due to the ambient environment, and there is a solution to it, which I have demonstrated. If the claim is that a stack overflow implies a bad design, then does a long running loop imply one as well? I could have hand translate a stack overflowing recursion into a long running loop. They are equivalent.

In practice, our program needs to accommodate user inputs as much as possible. If we were to give a bound on user inputs, it should be for some explainable business reason, not "sorry, our system only allocates 4MB stack size, so we don't allow you to build a term over a 128 depth".

```quote
I am not saying the compiler should always perform this transformation. This is not the message I am trying to convey. What I am trying to explain here, is that the compiler should (and must) do something to enable a fully generalized, graceful solution to this problem. It is OK to let a separate crate to do the job (and it's OK to not be part of stdlib too), but the compiler so far lacks functionality to resolve this problem.
```

I would suggest defining the minimal necessary compiler features to achieve what you want, for example:
- [Control over drop semantics project goal](https://goals.rust-lang.org/2026/manually-drop-attr.html) - if it does what you need
- full detection of recursive calls
- macro-generated unique names
- panic elision
- *anything else you need*

Then asking what's already available, what's in development, and what would be accepted as an experiment.

To be honest, I find the docs hard to summarise, because they are very verbose, and low-information. (Or low in relevant information density.)

621518777.en:
@_**Jason Hu|320010** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/131828-t-compiler/topic/Drop.20causes.20stack.20overflow.20for.20deeply.20nested.20data.20structures/near/621490885):
```quote
If the claim is that a stack overflow implies a bad design, then does a long running loop imply one as well?
```

Depending on the problem domain, yes. My background is in hard realtime software, and recursion (especially unbounded) in that domain is just a no-go. But even looking at other fields I have worked in, such as writing reliable high performance server software it is not desirable.

What about single user programs? Well, again my experience is that when I have come across deeply recursive data structures that my representation has been wrong. For example when dealing with ASTs, flattening the structure according to data oriented design principled has resulted in a faster program than a pointer chasing recursive structure. And dropping then is just dropping the underlying Vec or arena, which is no longer recursive. It becomes at worst linear complexity in time and constant in RAM usage (and if drop is trivial, the time can also be constant complexity).

Just because you have something that is logically recursive doesn't mean that it has to be structurally recursive. And on modern CPUs with cache the linearised approach is genrally superior thanks to better prefetching.

621526578.en:
@**teor** It also really depends on what your question is. If the question is about how to prevent Drop from causing stack overflow, then I am not sure Control over Drop is the way to go for the drop problem alone. In general, a recursive data's drop requires touch data as large as its size, so an iterative version of drop should also be able to keep track of all data too. The crux is the size of data is unknown without a thorough traversal, so some memory allocation is needed to maintain dynamic data structure.  

However, the way I see this drop problem, is that it is not different from tackling stack overflow due to any recursion. Ideally, the transformation is the best performed on MIR. This is the timing where all resolution has happened. Here, a CPS transformation is the most accurate and the guarantee of program equivalence is the easiest.

I see that's probably not possible for what rustc is today. The next best solution is the perform the transformation on type-checked HIR. In general, to perform accurate transformation, both type and borrow information needs to be available. To name a few:
1. Name resolution. This is to handle trait impls, where `Trait::<S>foo` and `Trait::<T>foo` are distinguished. Fully detection of recursive call sites also requires this.
2. Life time information. This is to maintain drop order consistency.
3. Access to all function bodies. This is to handle recursions in lambda expressions passed into other function bodies.

621551066.en:
> Recursion is an elegant mathematical model on paper, sure. But code is not math. Code is engineering

I think you can frame both of these positions as being engineering ones. Handling unbounded recursion via allocation is the engineering position of "The program should complete its work if the memory required fits in available memory, without needing to transform every tree-traversing algorithm or tune the stack size". And, in fact, `rustc` does this with `stacker`. A difference in context that this is a reasonable option for “trusted input” batch jobs, whereas strictly bounded resource consumption is important for "untrusted input", servers, and real-time applications.

621682781.en:
I’m not sure what you mean by “built-in”. The `impl Drop for Value`, if any, is library code in serde_json. There is compiler generated drop glue that can recurse, but this can be defused by doing the (iterative) dropping in `impl Drop` while replacing `*self` with a simple value for which the drop glue won’t recurse.

It’s true that you can’t write that `impl Drop` in another library, but the same is true for every other operation implemented in serde_json — in general you need the library’s cooperation for handling deeply nested values without stack overflow. In this particular case, since it’s a fully public enum, you can probably do whatever you need without running any serde_json code (e.g., you can side-step the recursive drop problem for any type of your own that owns a `Value`). But if the type is more opaque, you probably have a similar problem for both Drop and for other APIs that can’t be implemented outside the library. For example, if the `PartialEq` or `Debug` impl for nested Values overflows the stack, you also can’t fix that from the outside, other than by avoiding it and re-implementing it iteratively, which is only possible for `Value` because it doesn’t hide any variants/fields/other types that could be involved in the recursion.

621684895.en: Ah, per https://github.com/serde-rs/json/issues/440 it would be semver breaking for serde_json to add a `impl Drop for Value`. Unfortunate. 613940777.en:
The CRATE_HASH regex in compiletest doesn't care about the length, so it's only triggered in specific circumstances:
- the compiletest regex doesn't match
  - compiletest seems to match the UI test "crate" disambiguator reliably, but not other positions like Type<alloc[hex chars]::Box>
- the UI test uses v0 demangling
- the UI test uses a custom normalization regex that expects exactly 16 hex characters
- the crate disambiguator is 15 characters (happens on 1/16 changes to each crate hash)

It's possible it was dismissed as a spurious failure, and then a subsequent rollup modified the crate hash so it had 16 characters again. It's also possible no tests existed that triggered it until I added this line:
https://github.com/teor2345/rust/blob/511d2920c48fac1afc67b628a5b5125c880f243b/tests/ui/splat/splat-mangling.rs#L185

It's also possible we changed LowerHex formatting to omit leading zeroes at some point. Or omit a single leading zero. (If it was only omitting leading zero *bytes*, then it would only happen in 1/256 changes to the crate hash.)

620917525.en:
The infra team wants to remove all individual and team ownership from `rust-lang` crates.io crates, to reduce the attack surface of someone's account being compromised. The idea is that we will:
- Enable trusted publishing for these crates, so that they can only be published from CI of their repositories.
- Remove all team and individual access, so that only `rust-lang-owner` actually owns the crate on crates.io.
- Track which teams (virtually) "own" the corresponding crates in the `team` database.
- Implement a Zulip command for yanking/unyanking a crate in a public Zulip topic, which will only be allowed for members of teams attached to those crates in the `team` database.

I wanted to give a heads-up to the Compiler team about this plan, and ask if you have any feedback/concerns. Currently, the Compiler team owns 16 crates on crates.io (https://crates.io/teams/github:rust-lang:compiler).

620098234.en:
Recently, I have been looking at removing unnecessary allocations from rustc. One thing that comes up repeatedly is an opportunity to use a simple ever-growing arena, instead of using repeated nested allocations on the heap. Using a `Vec` for that is fine, but often we don't even really need to produce a slice of the items in the arena, and moving all the inner things when reallocating can be a waste.

The canonical solution for that is to have a Vec of chunks, where you allocate a chunk (of the same size, if you want to support random indexing access), and then when you run out of space, you allocate a new chunk, and thus you don't need to move all the previous items.

This is implemented e.g. in the `segmented_vec` crate, but I was wondering whether there is anything like that already in the compiler? It seems like a very useful thing, but I wasn't able to find a generic data structure in rustc that would implement something like this already. It doesn't help that this (AFAIK) doesn't have a clear nomenclature in the data structure world (it can be called chunked vec, segmented vec, etc.).

620099332.en: On this subject, note that "same-sized chunks" is not necessary for random access indexing. The other kind of segmented vector with O(1) indexing has exponentially growing segments (segment `i` holds `1 << i` elements). This removes or reduce the need to manage a variable-sized collection of segment pointers since you can always allocate ceil(log2(max capacity)) segment pointers up-front (though you may want not want to do that for small vectors). And if you do it right, it basically just replaces the div/mod by pow2 for indexing with ilog2 (ca. same cost as count leading zeros), shift, subtract.

620108789.en: Speaking of append-only vec, I have experimented in the past (not for rustc) with representing a "`Vec` that you only append to" as pair (pointer to next free slot, remaining capacity) and moving the total capacity into the heap allocation. That relies on a phase separation between appending and indexing/iteration, and in return produces a bit less code for the "append" parts than passing `&mut Vec` around (mostly because you can pass two words in registers and so can arrange for APIs that don't round-trip the Vec fields through memory so much). But I never finished that because it didn't help as much as I hoped without `extern "rust-cold"` ABI and without extensive (mechanical) rewrites of the code that appends to the vector.

453845868.en:
Someone on Reddit was complaining about incremental build times on large projects, and made the brave claim that they would be okay with no inlining at all in the changed code.

So I'm going to try to clean up the monomorphization code so that it is possible to configure the compiler to lower everything (or nearly everything) as GloballyShared, with 1 item per CGU. Right now the logic for deciding on the instantiation mode is spread across the compiler, and I'm going to try to centralize it into `cross_crate_inlinable` or a companion function that takes an `Instance` instead.

As far as I can tell so far, this is going to involve landing a lot of small cleanup-y probably-perf-sensitive PRs. I intend to land basically the entire effort in little PRs that are merged on their own merits, because I know others have pointed out that the instantiation mode selection needs some love. I'm just starting this topic to let people know what I'm up to :smile: 

The first two of these PRs are
https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/128165
https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/128170

608316049.en:
It dictates things like stack alignment at function entry, or the alignment of functions themselves, and also it dictates FPCSR and MXCSR's value at function entry. A function that is publicly callable must have certain values set in those registers at function entry to be conformant to the ABI. This is part of how LLVM can assume the default, or at least how it can get away with it: because actually it has to be.

In particular, on Windows, their "long double", last I checked, is just `f64`. Please feel free to correct me on this. It does, on "x86-32", use the floating point stack to pass values, because that was what was available, so it passes them in 80-bit registers. However, they perform the operations according to FPCSR, which makes the operations happen according to a significantly reduced precision. Namely, they are as close as possible to simply approximating `binary64` as that hardware supports.

There's obviously other reasons like "you usually don't need as many predicates at a time as values". 608328740.en: Anyway, regarding what to do here: I don't think it would be the *worst* thing to say that x87_f80 only exists on platforms where that's what `long double` is, since presumably those coincide with platforms that aren't potentially miscompiled. 608653158.en:
As for i686, I don't think the ABI makes a guarantee in the first place, because DirectX exists.

`IDirect3D9::CreateDevice` takes a `BehaviorFlags` parameter, and one of those flags is `D3DCREATE_FPU_PRESERVE`:

> Set the precision for Direct3D floating-point calculations to the precision used by the calling thread. If you do not specify this flag, Direct3D defaults to single-precision round-to-nearest mode for two reasons:
> * Double-precision mode will reduce Direct3D performance.
> * Portions of Direct3D assume floating-point unit exceptions are masked; unmasking these exceptions may result in undefined behavior.

Yes, DirectX used to set the FPCSR precision to _PC_24 by default. It was as fun as you could imagine.

619651653.en:
> not sure if any of these can happen?

The first two problems would also affect our current workaround for the `"Rust"` ABI. In practice this doesn't happen because if LLVM realises it can change the function signature it will also change the calling convention to `fastcc`, which returns floats in SSE registers and is therefore unaffected by the issue. All LLVM floating point libcalls are for mathematical operations which are allowed to quieten signalling NaNs (`abs`, `copysign` and negation are never libcalls), so the calling convention isn't an issue there.

622074620.en:
Currently, `VaArgSafe` is defined as:
```rust
pub impl(self) unsafe trait VaArgSafe {}
```
Notably, there's no `: Sized` supertrait. As a result, it's legal (if not very useful) to write `dyn VaArgSafe`. Is it worth adding a `:Sized` supertrait to prevent such code?

Note that `VaArgSafe` is stabilizing in 1.99.0 (current beta, stabilizing October 1)

The kernel has its own atomics implementation using inline assembly, and we explicitly never want any code anywhere using LLVM atomics (that is `core::sync::atomic`). We handle the aarch64 LSE atomic stuff with that inline asm manually.

621649571.en: e.g. on AArch32 VMSA (e.g. Cortex-A) where load/store exclusive doesn't work until the MMU is enabled and the memory is marked as Normal. Or on the Raspberry Pi RP2350 where load/store exclusive always fails when the value is placed into external PSRAM.
621649571.zh: e.g. on AArch32 VMSA (e.g. Cortex-A) where load/store exclusive doesn't work until the MMU is enabled and the memory is marked as Normal. Or on the Raspberry Pi RP2350 where load/store exclusive always fails when the value is placed into external PSRAM.

621649791.en: if you /did have such static atomics, I'd want them to be in well defined linker sections so I can use the linker to move them to memory ranges that I know will work, and I'd want to know precisely when they would be accessed so I could avoid such APIs until after the MMU is enabled.

617848955.en:
You'd need a feature like this:
```rust
fn foo(a: &mut u32) -> &'{*a} u32 { // must return a shared reborrow of `a`
  a
}
```

Now the caller can see that the lifetime of `&mut u32` isn't captured, but its place is reborrowed as shared at exit. The caller can therefore reuse the original borrow as shared together with the result.

```quote
cc @**RalfJ** here - is my read of what take_mut does in line with your understanding?
```

no. :)
you are conflating the opsem concept of "uninit memory" with the logical concept of "bytes whose invariants expresses ownership that I hold". `take_mut` does not mutate the contents of the `&mut` until the end when it puts in the new `T`, so they are not uninit in the opsem sense. in particular, the validity invariant of those contents holds at every point.
the *library* invariant may not hold, because ownership has been taken out. but that's a very different situation.

618218948.en: I shared my thoughts on this (https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/4000#discussion_r3839091267) on github, but I would still argue that `Box` and `&own` should have the same semantics as to whether `take` is valid. I'm in favour of saying that `take` *is* valid on both and you aren't allowed to look at an enum discriminant after you've moved out of the enum value. The alternative would be to change the API of `Box::take` to instead leave behind a `Box<WriteOnly<T>>` or the likes. either way i'd... honestly rather axe `Box::take` as it is now than give up on unifying semantics here
618218948.zh: I shared my thoughts on this (https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/4000#discussion_r3839091267) on github, but I would still argue that `Box` and `&own` should have the same semantics as to whether `take` is valid. 🟧 This is an obligatory thread to make sure that my spicy opinions aren't actually too spicy.

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/161879#issuecomment-5502815906

IPv6 is 28 years old. The fact that the world is still stuck on IPv4, and we're discussing this change on a site that doesn't even support IPv6 (GitHub), is a problem worth rectifying. This change proposes updating the docs for version-ambiguous IP address APIs to use IPv6 addresses instead of IPv4 addresses by default.

There are some places where we could include both, and maybe that is preferable in some cases. But my opinion is that if someone is explicitly looking at APIs that support IPv6 addresses and they're in any way confused or put off by seeing IPv6 addresses without their IPv4 equivalents, that is their own problem they need to rectify. And I'm going further and saying that basically every argument I've seen from people online claiming that IPv4 is somehow superior to IPv6 in some particular use case just doesn't understand how IPv6  works, is resistant to change, or doesn't like not being able to remember their IP address any more. (That last one is a skill issue, but also technically a privacy issue as well, since it requires disabling SLAAC privacy extensions.)

So, I'm fine signing off on this change as-is but going to wait in case the author wants to work on making some of the docs show both versions instead. And want to make sure that this is a reasonable opinion and not a case of needing to pour some milk on my spicy take.

620555506.en:
I recently ran into some cases in Cargo where joining paths (`PathBuf`s) was hot, and the solution was pretty much to replace
```rust
let p: PathBuf = get_path();
return p.join(path);
```

with
```rust
let p: PathBuf = get_path();
p.push(path)
return p;
```

Since `join` takes `&Path(Buf)`, the original allocation cannot be reused, even though you then throw away the `PathBuf`. This is quite wasteful, because if you do `a.join(b).join(c).join(d)`, which is common when you need to join multiple paths, you just reallocate and drop PathBufs over and over again.

In theory this could be solved via some structural sharing inside `PathBuf`, but that's likely overkill for the stdlib.

But what about an owned variant of `push`, which would consume the original `PathBuf` and reuse its allocation? Or does something like that exist and I missed it?

620785668.en:
Hi all, I noticed that the "Move generic functionality from AtomicT to Atomic<T>" goal of the tracking issue for generic Atomic hasn't been touched in a while so I figured I'd give it a whirl.

There is an issue that I've noticed, and I'm not sure how to handle it so I'm hoping someone here can direct me. The problem is that the same function can have differing stability attributes depending on the type. Take for example the `new` function, for integer atomics both the normal and const form were stabilized with 1.34.0, but for AtomicPtr the function is marked as introduced in 1.0.0, and const stabilized in 1.24.0.

So far I've broken up my implementation depending on target support, so all the stuff that requires target_has_atomic_load_store is under a separate impl block from target_has_atomic for example. I did this through introducing some new traits, and I guess I could do the same do the same thing to match the stability attributes that currently exist but that would result in a lot of new traits being added and the code being very messy in general. Does anyone have insights on how I can handle this?

@_**Benjamin Saunders|216097** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/219381-t-libs/topic/Is.20Arc.3CMutex.3CT.3E.3E.20specialized.3F/near/618682515):
```quote
my understanding is that `Mutex`(at least on some platforms) has an internal heap allocation to hold its state at a stable address
```

I believe on some targets, the lock itself needs to be heap allocated, but on major platforms (linux, windows, macos) this is not the case. The `T` value is stored inline in all cases, only the lock state (typically as a `pthread_mutex_t`) is outlined on some targets.
You can't really specialize this case, because `Arc<Mutex<T>>` needs to be able to supply a `&Mutex<T>`.  It's also going to have diminishing returns anyways, since there's no need on the most common platforms.

618913232.en: Here’s a second API-design reason why an `ArcMutex` *shouldn’t* exist: there are often use cases for having a portion of the `Arc`-shared data *not* be mutable, and be borrowable without taking the lock, by putting it in the `Arc` but outside the `Mutex`. If `ArcMutex` were seen as one thing, then it would be harder to see that opportunity, and harder to refactor.

Yes, with the caveat that anything reference counted can have contention on the reference counter. The most extreme example I have seen was s program of mine processing debuginfo in parallel (using rayon), where a single (read only) Arc was 36 % of the *total* runtime. Needless to say I redesigned with borrows instead to avoid that overhead. Significantly more complicated (and needed some unsafe) but worth it.

As much as I dislike Windows, at least it isn't classic MacOS (which I grew up with) that used `:` as the separator and `::` as `..`

622097812.en:
I'm arguing the transformation is legal, because every possible execution of the transformed program yields results unobservable distinct from the original (under time traveling).  Specifically, it yields a result that cannot be proved incorrect for one of two reasons:
1. The println terminates, the implementation chose 47, and UB lets the implementation do whatever it wants throughout the whole "trace", The fact that the implementation prints the "wrong" value is just a consequence of UB.
2. The println does not terminate, and nothing after it happens - no blah print, no UB. The implementation didn't print the wrong value because it chose the right one.

To be clear, I'm not concerned that this is allowed under non-time travelling. The reasoning depends on time-traveling. The concern I have is: Are we sure that nothing does or relies on similar reasoning?
This was my attempt to create an (albeit contrived) example of an optimization that relies on the ability for UB to "time travel" without relying on any I/O operation to return.

622100580.en:
By argument is the assumption about the pairing of an execution to an environment. Something the implementation has under its control. Ultimately, a transformation from one Language to another doesn't need to preserve the full semantics of the input, it just needs to respect as-if. The result needs to correspond to one possible execution for a given input, and if for a given input/environment *any* execution exhibits UB, the entire behaviour is undefined.
This is the pre-time-travelling definition of UB.

622115214.en:
@_**niluxv|401145** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/136281-t-opsem/topic/Interesting.20Consequence.20of.20time.20traveling.20UB/near/622111310):
```quote
Time-travelling-UB means that `trace + (out(x), UB)` and `trace + (UB)` are equivalent traces for every trace `trace` and value `x`.
```

under some guesses as to what you mean by that notation (I assume that's not a tuple of `out(x)` and `UB`), makes sense. typically what we do is we just say there's a single "UB" trace and when a program triggers UB, the entire trace it emitted so far gets replaced by that "UB" trace.
(we assume here that `out` is the only kind of event on the trace. if there's also `in` things get more complicated.)

> It has nothing to do with whether some function possibly diverges.

Yes it does. if you define UB in the time-traveling way above, then it becomes correct for a compiler to assume that `print` (the primitive that emits the `out` event) is `willreturn`. (`willreturn` here stands for a semantic property of operations that boils down to, the code that after this operation is guaranteed to be executed -- or equivalently, 'pure modulo UB' operations can be moved up across a `willreturn` operation.) if you define UB in a way that it's just an event at the end of a trace, but the events before it in the trace also matter, then it becomes wrong for a compiler to assume that `print` is `willreturn`.
whether or not some function diverges is not part of the definition, but the effect on `willreturn` is a consequence of the definition. this depends on the definition of `willreturn` of course. the property that a compiler cares about when it asks for `willreturn` is reordering stuff from after to before, so that is the definition I would use. I admit I was not explicit about that.

621898220.en: At least I don't see what [story you can tell](https://www.ralfj.de/blog/2026/03/13/inline-asm.html) about a `black_box`-like inline asm block that gives you any useful guarantee here. If you specify the asm as pass-through, then there's actually no constraint on what the compiler may do. If you specify it as possibly returning a different value than is passed in, then your program is incorrect according to that spec. And specifying it as having some side effect doesn't affect how "pure" operations can be compiled around it.

Yes, we can't rely on a register of the right size being present, so larger values would either have to still spill, or split into multiple registers if it's still reasonably small (in the linked issue, see how the `16 =>` branch is handled—IDK if it's worth handling more than this, but this much is nice as it means something like `&[T]` stays in registers).

When `black_box` was `asm!`, this kind of thing was impossible to do correctly (in generic code), due to `asm!` not supporting `MaybeUninit` input/output. But presumably (hopefully) that's not an issue at the point when we're deciding what the intrinsic turns into.

622260386.en:
Last I heard whether or not we add `freeze` was very much still up in the air (although I'm very much in favor of it). Using freeze for this would be possible[^1] if we were to write `black_box` in userspace (err, in library code), but I don't see why we wouldn't keep it as an intrinsic.

[^1]: Note that given that the signature is (likely) `MaybeUninit<T>::freeze(self) -> MaybeUninit<T>` and `MaybeUninit<T>` and `T` have the same ABI (or at least on copy will still deinit the padding bytes of `T`, AFAIK), you would have to first convert `T` to a POD (in the `bytemuck::Pod` sense) type before doing the freeze. So it would be awkward. This is neither here nor there, though, I suppose.

598415849.en:
My unsubstantiated gut feeling is that subobject provenance is probably not worth it for the long tail of capricious gotchas when writing unsafe code that it would likely cause. On the other hand, more than once I've stared at some code that passes a pointer to one field of an ADT into a function, and looking at some access to *other* fields around the call, and thinking that subobject provenance would be really nice for letting LLVM optimize those other accesses better.

For example, [this code](https://github.com/hanna-kruppe/chacha8rand/blob/fbd14b30f7030e7d0a227db177a7630687c6e177/chacha8rand/src/lib.rs#L823-L824) does an indirect call to refill a buffer that's a field of `self`, then resets another field of `self` (index into that buffer) to zero. Semantically, the order of these two steps doesn't matter. But at least for rustc+LLVM as it stands now, it's not clear that the indirect call can't change the counter, so the current order is better because it makes obvious that the counter will be zero after a refill. I'm not sure if protectors or other parts of a Rust aliasing model would help with this.

598436674.en: I think arrays/slices are a bigger issue in practice for sub-object provenance than structs. There's a lot of code out there that takes the address of one element of an array, turns it into a raw pointer and then expects to be able to access any element of the array with it. Ideally such code should be using `&raw`, but that syntax is relatively new and a lot of existing code just creates a normal reference and casts that to a pointer.

598438266.en: An interesting data point is Swift which is [even stricter](https://www.cocoawithlove.com/blog/2016/02/16/use_it_or_lose_it_why_safe_c_is_sometimes_unsafe_swift.html) than what is being proposed here. In Swift taking the address of a field "materializes" that field only for the scope of the borrow. Not only does this mean that you can't access other fields through that pointer, it also means that if you take the address of 2 fields adjacent of a local then there is no guarantee that they have consecutive addresses.

598440392.en:
I think for structs there's still code that does this. For example, when I started with Rust I did stuff like
```rs
#[repr(C)]
pub struct Vec3 {
    pub x: f32,
    pub y: f32,
    pub z: f32,
}
```
And then use `&v.x as *const f32` (or mut) to access all 3 elements of `v` like an array. This is not strictly allowed in C/C++ either, but doing it is common. That said, I haven't written code like this in a long time (I'm well aware that `v as *const _ as *const f32` is the way to do that), but it wouldn't surprise me at all if there's code out there that does this. In fact, it would surprise me quite a bit if there is not.

599106666.en: General subobject provenance in LLVM is kind of Hard, because it adds a lot of intrinsics on the pointer path, and everything needs to learn to look past them (correctly), otherwise you lose optimizations. I think your case might be handled more easily if we add allocator provenance intrinsics (I guess this also more directly represents what you are doing, where multiple sub-allocations are serviced from one larger one). In that case looking through the intrinsics shouldn't be important. (The subobject provenance issue may become simpler if we add ptr_provenance path as part of full restrict.)

602695929.en:
Stumbled across this and these are my thoughts from the CHERI world:

CHERI can support this in the architecture, and so in CHERI LLVM it is a compile-time option to enable (for C/C++), with various type and member annotations, and builtins, to opt out in specific cases when otherwise enabled. This does brush up against language semantics issues (e.g. &a[x] is defined to be equivalent to a + x in C so shouldn't be restricted, and yet there are clearly reasons why that might be useful to do), as well as just de-facto use (e.g. embedding linked list nodes into larger structures), so our default is to turn it off, and if you want to turn it on you can, with varying degrees of aggressiveness that increasingly violate ISO C yet have clear benefits for certain use cases (like the array example, which you have to dial things up quite a bit to get). For our CheriBSD kernel we turn it on, as there is a non-zero number of past CVEs for overflowing within a struct, but only at the lowest level. Even then it is a decent source of friction (the cause of most of our panics these days when exercising previously-untested device drivers etc), but we currently view it as a worthwhile thing to do. I would hope that Rust would be better poised to be able to have a subobject provenance story in its semantics, but I know well the pain that can come from imposing such constraints on systems code...

602853007.en:
I am outside of opsem and only a little chic of a Rust developer so I don't think my vibes count for much but... I must say I actually do find myself thinking that I'd prefer having subobject provenance.

I find myself thinking that lacking subobject provenance sounds harder to reason about in unsafe code, or harder to teach maybe...? Like, you have an unsafe operation that takes some `&T` and its safety condition is that this must have been created in a particular way / from a particular struct, and also must not have had its provenance restricted, but none of that is visible in the type system. Effectively, the safest of safe types can now have fairly gnarly variance to when they're actually safe, and Rust just says: "yes, this is fine and if you want to write your unsafe code to work with references to a field of type T that just looks like a normal reference to a T, then knock yourself out."

Compared to having subobject provenance, where a reference is a reference is a reference, and if you want to do fancy and unsafe things with eg. field pointers then you have to write specific wrappers over field pointers and carefully carry the provenance over. A `&u32` is always just a `&u32` in this world, never a `&u32<MyStruct::field>`.

Sometimes you can't even statically write down the type that the header is part of. I don't think it's obvious that that kind of unsafe code would become much simpler to reason about by enforcing subobject provenance.

602863390.en:
I'm not smart enough and probably too tired to really understand but... In a sense I feel like this makes _safe_ code harder to write.

```rust
fn do_with_type_erased_t(t: &Header) { ... }
```

Is this function safe? Or did we make a mistake and it should actually be `unsafe`? That depends:
1. If it does not read anything beyond the Header then it is safe.
2. If it does read beyond the Header and we do not have subobject provenance it is also safe.
3. Exception: If we have a safe `fn restrict_provenance` in which case it must be unsafe.
4. Exception to 3: If we have a marker trait `Restrictable` that a type can opt out of which is required to call `fn restrict_provenance` then it is safe.
5. Alternative exception to 3: If `fn restrict_provenance` is unsafe then the function is again safe. The safety precondition on `restrict_provenance` is going to be pretty rough though; "reference must not be used to access data out of its bounds". That just feels like it's on the wrong end of the stick - proving a negative instead of giving a positive guarantee.

It just seems complicated to me that `&(mut )T` of all types would have a potentially viral safety condition like this.

@_**RalfJ|120791** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/136281-t-opsem/topic/Vibes.20on.20subobject.20provenance/near/602795996):
```quote
@**Jessica Clarke** is the point that enforcing subobject provenance is useful to find real bugs (that would be bugs even if the language had no subobject provenance)?
```

It's about closing security vulnerabilities that are due to intra-object overflows, like https://projectzero.google/2021/12/this-shouldnt-have-happened.html. In theory if you turn on subobject bounds with CHERI LLVM when compiling that code then (ignoring that the next step in the chain was to inject a function pointer which we'd also break, but surely there are other interesting data-oriented things you could do) CHERI could have prevented it. Sometimes there are good reasons why you don't want subobject provenance, but I generally take the view that it's the exception not the rule and it's not too onerous to require opting into the less-secure form, but at least in the case of C there is a lot of existing code that would break so the story is more awkward. With Rust though I imagine (or at least naively hope...) people are generally better about not doing things that go against subobject provenance than your average overly-cunning C programmer.

It's about closing security vulnerabilities that are due to intra-object overflows, like https://projectzero.google/2021/12/this-shouldnt-have-happened.html. In theory if you turn on subobject bounds with CHERI LLVM when compiling that code then (ignoring that the next step in the chain was to inject a function pointer which we'd also break, but surely there are other interesting data-oriented things you could do) CHERI could have prevented it. Sometimes there are good reasons why you don't want subobject provenance, but I generally take the view that it's the exception not the rule and it's not too onerous to require opting into the less-secure form, but at least in the case of C there is a lot of existing code that would break so the story is more awkward. With Rust though I imagine (or at least naively hope...) people are generally better about not doing things that go against subobject provenance than your average overly-cunning C programmer.

by that I mean that just like the compiler can't put `T` in read-only memory if it contains an `UnsafeCell` ignoring stuff behind pointers, I think the compiler shouldn't enable subobject provenance if `T` contains any type with subobject provenance disabled, ignoring stuff behind pointers. I'm not saying that some other unrelated field of `T` gets disabled subobject provenance too, which is the undecided part of `UnsafeCell`. e.g.:
```rust
pub struct T {
    pub unrelated: Unrelated,
    pub field: TypeWithoutSubobjectProvenance,
}
```
so with `t: T` -- `&t` doesn't use subobject provenance, neither does `&t.field`, but `&t.unrelated` can use subobject provenance since `Unrelated` doesn't disable it.

@_**Jules Bertholet|421518** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/136281-t-opsem/topic/Vibes.20on.20subobject.20provenance/near/603950737):
```quote
C's flexible array member pattern is commonly used from Rust in a way that would violate subobject provenance: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-bindgen/using-fam.html
```

They don't inherently violate subobject provenance, and you can still restrict references in the abstract machine to be only to the array, but you do need a way to talk about the size of that subobject in the semantics (and, for enforcement, obtain it somehow). For us, C flexible array members (and I think zero-sized ones as well, since zero-sized arrays are a GNU extension that often get used for flexible arrays in pre-C99 code) with subobject bounds enabled notionally get bounds of the entire flexible array member, which we realise by leaving the upper bound from the surrounding object as-is, only increasing the lower bond, which is a conservative over-approximation (since depending on where that capability came from there may be other objects beyond the end of that flexible array member which will end up within bounds, but it's the best we can do without further annotations like the `__counted_by` used by Apple's -fbounds-safety software bounds enforcement).

based on the discussion above and at the recent t-opsem meeting, it seems like at least 3 out of 5 opsem members would be fine with saying "there is no subobject provenance on types that currently exist in the language, except maybe for enums". The main arguments are
- a bunch of existing code assumes this already for arrays and slices
- a lot of code generated by bindgen assumes this at least for repr(C) structs
- `#[repr]` shouldn't affect the opsem in such subtle ways
- the benefits of this UB are unclear. there are optimizations one can sketch where this is useful, but the fact that LLVM has no way of even representing this makes it look like there's no that much to be had here in terms of practically useful optimizations.

@**Crystal Durham** @**Mario Carneiro** you weren't at that meeting -- I wonder what your thoughts on this are?

607202157.en: I don't think LLVM's SRoA currently does this, but it's possible to promote some fields of an aggregate to SSA values while still keeping the original local, if subobject provenance proves that the escaping pointers can only access a subset of fields. For example, for a local `pair: (u32, f32)` where only `&pair.0` escapes, all mentions of `pair.1` could be redirected to a separate local `pair_1: f32`. This effectively takes subobject provenance reasoning and recasts it into separate objects to help LLVM's object-based provenance reasoning.

In the Rust version LLVM can't prove that accesses through `elements` don't also access `start`, which means that on every loop iteration it must write `start` back to memory so that the access via `elements` sees the correct value. The C++ version with TBAA doesn't have this problem because the individual elements of `elements` and `start` have different types. If you change the C++ code to have an array of `size_t` instead of `double` then it also loses the optimization and has to write back `start` on every loop iteration.

In the Rust version LLVM can't prove that accesses through `elements` don't also access `start`, which means that on every loop iteration it must write `start` back to memory so that the access via `elements` sees the correct value. The C++ version with TBAA doesn't have this problem because the individual elements of `elements` and `start` have different types. If you change the C++ code to have an array of `size_t` instead of `double` then it also loses the optimization and has to write back `start` on every loop iteration.

607255273.en:
We could say that if a local of an SRoA-eligible struct type does not have its address taken at any point, then its individual fields are treated as separate locals and can have offsets that differ from what the struct layout would prescribe. ("Does not have its address taken at any point" would be defined syntactically; e.g. an `&local` anywhere in the source, even in dead code, amounts to "taking the address".)

There are plenty of reasons why this particular approach might not be a good idea—making `&local` have spooky-action-at-a-distance among them—but hopefully it demonstrates that this is *possible* to support, and maybe there's a cleaner way.

````quote
@_**RalfJ|120791** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/136281-t-opsem/topic/Vibes.20on.20subobject.20provenance/near/607567862):
````
I dont see any thing in the standard permitting those to be used to do ptr arithmetic outside of arrays

[6.3.2.3 Pointers, item 7](https://www.iso-9899.info/n3047.html#6.3.2.3)
```quote
When a pointer to an object is converted to a pointer to a character type, the result points to the lowest addressed byte of the object. Successive increments of the result, up to the size of the object, yield pointers to the remaining bytes of the object.
```
Which yes, relies on &x.foo not being a restricted to a subobject (otherwise you could argue that it doesn't even let you access the next array element). While I agree with that q&a that this is unclear rather than clearly unrestricted, certainly the default assumption by programmers has been that it is unrestricted.

uintptr_t would rely on Footnote 73, which is just a footnote - "The mapping functions for converting a pointer to an integer or an integer to a pointer are intended to be consistent with the addressing structure of the execution environment." Otherwise pointer/int casting is at least allowed to be encrypt/decrypt, which would break using it for pointer math (since uintptr_t is only required to work for the same value pointer->int->pointer).

```quote
I don't see it as inflicting extra UB on everyone everywhere, I see it as inflicting a weird model of validity on everyone everywhere
```

we allow *tons* of things the safety invariant strictly forbids. we have a "memory contains untyped bytes" model even though our safety invariants would naturally give rise to "memory contains typed objects" -- but we recognize that people need to work with those bytes so we get out of their way to the extent that we can. your arguments based on naturality of subobject provenance only make sense to me if we assume a framework of typed memory. in a world where untyped memory has been accepted as the natural state of affairs, I cannot see at all how subobject provenance leads to a *less* weird model of validity.

"subobject provenance" has "object" in its name -- it's coherent with "memory contains typed objects" but rather unnatural in "memory contains untyped bytes". The uncanny valley in between typed and untyped memory does not seem to be a good place to be in.

607756036.en:
I guess that the answer changes in the `fn bar` case by "forking" the original `x: &mut _` reference into multiple references `&mut x[0]` and `&mut x[1]` - in a world without subobject provenance both of these would have write access to the entirety of the array `x` but that "other forked reference" limits what they can actually do without triggering UB. Compared to just holding the original `&mut x` and a derived `&mut x[1]`, we of course do not consider these two references aliasing since the original one is "turned off" while the derived one lives.

I personally cannot really say I like this from a surface language point of view, ... but at least we (hopefully) don't lose optimisations like in the last `fn inner` if we can argue that forking references does effectively produce a restricted form of subobject provenance.

@_**Mario Carneiro|271719** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/136281-t-opsem/topic/Vibes.20on.20subobject.20provenance/near/607833205):

And that's essentially CHERI's model: flat memory where capabilities are mostly an address and a window where that address is usable. The question is what's the window of a new pointer?

Today it's the allocation for pointers returned by the global allocator, and that same allocation for derived pointers. The rationale being what Ralf said: offsets between allocation is dynamic, offsets within allocations is (usually) static. Of course if you implement an allocator within an allocation (like a custom allocator), then that rationale doesn't work anymore because offsets between custom allocations are dynamic but still share the same window inherited from the global allocation they are drawn from.

The second question is whether we can change that, to which there's at least 2 options:
1. Explicit: the user may shrink the window when creating a new pointer (by default it inherits the window), which could be in the form of `restrict_provenance`.
2. Implicit: pointers (or maybe just references, TBD) get a window based on their type (possibly depending on attributes on the outer/inner types).

The problem of "implicit windowing" is legacy code (if the attributes are not opt-in). The problem of "explicit windowing" is optimizations (which are not "enabled by default"). Which is why it seems to all boil down to how much legacy would break and how much optimization would we get (to which I have no ideas, but according to the thread and AFAICT: non-negligible legacy would break and no clear optimizations except for enums)

607941879.en:
@_**Jacob Lifshay|229517** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/136281-t-opsem/topic/Vibes.20on.20subobject.20provenance/near/607907508):
```quote
if we expect people to be able to opt-out of subobject provenance and have `&Header` work when passed through safe code, `restrict_provenance` needs to be `unsafe` or do nothing on `&Header`, since otherwise `read_after_header(restrict_provenance(get_header()))` is UB
```

There could be a world in which you have both of:
* a `restrict_provenance` that becomes a no-op when used on `&T where T: NoSubobjectProvenance`, and
* a different such function that *fails to compile* in that case, because that’s a sign that you’ve done something broken with the ownership of a `T` like putting it in a `Box` that has none of the neighboring memory present

Though, hm, that’s another distinction in use cases, that one could want to make explicit, too. “This type may be used in a way which requires no-subobject-provenance” vs. “this type *is always* used in a way which requires no-subobject-provenance". The latter would mean that trying to construct `Box<Header>` is a logical error potentially leading to unsoundness, and the former would not.

Is any of this worth doing instead of using (newtyped) raw pointers? I don’t know. But I am both skeptical about the usability of "just use raw pointers", and wanting to not live in the world where accessing out of bounds of a reference's referent is OK, which means I wish that Rust did have an explicit opt-out (or opt-in!) per type.

2. puts pressure on safe Rust to do odd things to regain said optimisations (like create a `&self.foo` and explicitly remove it after a cross-cutting call to prove no mutations, while hoping that the compiler doesn't use a stack slot on it),

3. seems to also be a slippery slope to Cells leaking interior mutability into their surroundings (`&Cell` has to assume bytes outside of it are also interior-mutable, hence `&StructContainingCell` has to kinda assume all of its fields are interior-mutable),

4. seems to be a fairly all-or-nothing thing, in that a hypothetical `fn restrict_provenance` or an attribute to do the same either has to be unsafe, or a function containing reference access expansion has to be unsafe with the precondition of said function or attribute not being used. (The attribute is easier if the library doesn't enable foreign code to create the referenced data.) Effectively, if a `&Header` reference may or may not be restricted (depending on if a `restrict_provenace` was called on it, of if it lives in a restricted struct?) then we have a risky reference validity condition (used by some functions) that is not visible in the type system. (I've generally preferred making newtypes for these cases so that I can see in the type system that I have less restricted access that the pointer referree type suggests.)

But as said above: I'm but a little chick and definitely don't know much about opsem, nor do I know that much about compiler optimisations. I also don't really know or understand if the ~6000? UB cases found with SB Miri is a lot or not, and therefore whether halving that to around 3000? IIRC with TB and no subobject provenance is a big deal or not.

```quote
Hot take: Rust already has subobject provenance https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ptr/index.html#allocation

Allocations essentially are a particularly strict form of subobjects. Using allocators on top of other allocators, you can have a build a whole tower of nested sub"objects" (allocations). 620073041.en:
```
I feel that an attribute on a field does make sense - it at least explains (to me) how the compiler could even optimise based on subobject provenance in a world where it is not a given. `&foo.header` touches a field with `#[header]`? => can't assume it won't touch `foo.data`. `&foo.part` doesn't have `#[header]`? => can assume it won't touch `foo.data`.

But a type-level opt-out also seems necessary: both for Thom's above case where the full object doesn't exist as a nameable Rust type, but also for `&array[0]` - if the `Type` in `array: Type[]` opts out of subobject provenance then we can happily say that the array does not have subobject provenance.

But none of this really helps existing code. If existing code has to be correct as-it-is while Rust gains opt-outable subobject provenance then it kinda seems like `#[repr(C)]` would be the only reasonable thing to rely on... If `#[repr(C)]` on a type automatically opts it out of subobject provenance but with some `#[get_it_back]` attribute in existence to opt it back then maybe it wouldn't be too odd that `#[repr(C)]` has strong effect on opsem: it's a default but not something that cannot be changed.

Having `#[repr(ordered_fields)]` increases in importance daily.

620074480.en:
Some examples:

```rust
#[repr(Rust)]
// or #[repr(ordered_fields)]
struct RStruct {
  r___restricted: RField, // Non-repr(C) field in a normal struct -> default to restricted subobject provenance
  #[unrestricted_references]
  r_unrestricted: RField, // Opt out of restricted subobject provenance
  c_unrestricted: CField, // repr(C) field in a normal struct -> default to unrestricted subobject provenance
  #[restricted_references]
  c___restricted: CField, // Opt back into restricted subobject provenance
}

#[repr(C)]
struct CStruct {
  r_unrestricted: RField, // Non-repr(C) field in a C struct -> default to unrestricted subobject provenance
  #[restricted_references]
  r___restricted: RField, // Opt back into restricted subobject provenance
  c_unrestricted: CField, // repr(C) in both sides -> unrestricted
  #[restricted_references]
  c___restricted: CField, // Opt back into restricted subobject provenance
}

#[repr(Rust)]
// or #[repr(ordered_fields)]
struct RField {}
#[repr(C)]
struct CField {}
```

620082598.en:
imo having type-level opt-out is quite useful since we already do that for other things (`PhantomPinned`/`UnsafeCell`) and for any struct type, if you're going to use the `Header` pattern, you'll want to mark the `Header` type since that's only one spot instead of the `N` structs that contain the `Header`.

That also helps Rust tell LLVM the right function argument attributes (which iirc doesn't currently have but could definitely gain -- something like `cant_access_outside(-23, 45)`) when you pass a `&Header` into a function, rather than Rust having to always tell LLVM it-could-be-a-header-pattern because it doesn't know if someone got that pointer from a field access and if that field was properly annotated with the opt-out or not.

619859216.en:
From LLVM's LangRef
```quote
Warning

Constant duplication currently makes it unsound to compare pointers if either may be `unnamed_addr`, because each reference to the global in the IR may return a different pointer, and optimization passes may create additional references. Optimization passes can also create pointer comparisons with the expectation that the comparison will return true if the object is the same, which theoretically can make any usage of `unnamed_addr` unsound, but in practice it is unlikely that input IR that does not explicitly compare pointers will be affected by this issue.
```
They obviously have a different meaning of "unsound" here but this still seems crazy to me. I would not expect a read-only `static` to randomly give me different addresses.

620775259.en:
At a face value I would say we cannot merge them, at least not under the as-if rule. In the opsem, that is, before any optimizations apply, if two pointers have the same address and you perform a load from both, then assuming neither load triggers UB, the two loads must return the same value. So from this you can conclude that the second allocation is also initialized *in the opsem*.

At least that is my understanding of the current opsem models.

620775501.en: And so merging leads us to conclude that the memory of the second allocation is initialized *in the opsem*. That is, programs assuming the value is initialized will not be UB under the opsem, and so such programs cannot be considered to rely on refinement of an execution with UB in the opsem.

If there wasn't an immutable shared borrow there, the compiler would have the burden of proving that overlapping the allocations does not cause operations on one to interfere with the other. However, the compiler can ignore, for the purposes of upholding that burden, any operation that would be UB, such as writing through a shared reference to bytes not inside an `UnsafeCell`.

Sorry for the long radio silence on this.

I originally intended to respond by proposing an alterative design that unifies the issues addressed in that PR with issues addressed in a number of other proposals. That alternative design is [here](https://gist.github.com/joshlf/2dbca0d5d025cfd0d40424ed3e50e0ed).

After very helpful feedback from @**Crystal Durham** and @**Ben Kimock (Saethlin)** during the last t-opsem meeting, I realized that I was biting off more than I could chew on my own.

I just finished a [draft proposal](https://gist.github.com/joshlf/8f6751869cd17fd4a0b5695877b05e21) that argues that we need *some* unified model for reasoning about questions of layout, ABI, etc. In particular, I argue that reasoning about these questions piecemeal continues to paint us further into design corners that we then have to make breaking changes to escape. I think we should do at least some thinking about a unified model before we make any more commitments in this space.

My plan is to post a comment to the same effect on that PR, but I first wanted to socialize this in a smaller group before I drop what is admittedly a grenade into the discussion.

(In terms of the PR itself, I am aware of a very minor risk of future incompatibility, which I'll raise. But more to the point, I argue in the proposal that we should be skeptical of our own ability to evaluate these things without a unified model, so I think we should move more carefully until we have such a model. "I can't think of any problems" has historically not been a good predictor of there not being problems.)

620108648.en:
I'm trying to thread a tricky needle here, and I don't claim to have the optimal approach:
- I don't want to try to stall everything (the perfect being the enemy of the good)
- I *do* want to get everyone involved in these discussions to start thinking of a unified model as something worth considering

I agree that Rust has historically handled these things incrementally. In some domains, that approach has been successful. However, IMO when it comes to layout, ABI, and other compatibility-with-the-external-world questions, that approach has frequently painted us into corners or resulted in implementations or feature designs which are just *wrong* wrt the external reality.

620115185.en: I hate to say this but I feel like the pre-RFCs and proposal would be much better if hand-authored. It's extremely verbose and repetitive (even for LLM-generated text it's a bit much, and to be clear I'm ignoring the appendices when I say this). We don't have a rule against LLM content that isn't for inclusion in rust-lang/rust (the forge document only applies there), but a pretty consistent note is that reading LLM generated text is fairly tiring, partially because of it's repetitiveness. I don't have a hard line against LLM use (I probably wouldn't complain if this were more reasonably sized), but this kind of thing seems a bit much to me, especially for three pre-RFCs and one proposal to come all at once (the note in the forge document that "LLMs work best when used as a tool to write *better*, not *faster*" feels relevant here to me).

I tried to structure the post as “brief argument” (Part I) followed by “exhaustive argument” (Part II) that goes through every instance of incompatibility. The exhaustive coverage was meant to demonstrate that the problem is real and persistent, not just the exception that proves the rule.

There are also a number of subtleties that I felt needed to be covered, and I wasn’t sure how to keep them concise, e.g.:
- Arguing that we need to consider forwards-evolvavility (to avoid issues present in some current proposals, which propose to change the semantics of things like `repr(C)`, which risks making unsafe code silently unsound)
- Explaining what a “unified model” might mean, since I explicitly *don’t* want to prescribe that it has to be reified as a model in rustc
- Forecasting future issues like multiple address spaces

614354140.en:
Closures (and coroutines) currently behave almost like normal ADTs. in particular, if they have fields of reference type, those get retagged as the closure / coroutine is moved around. This can cause gnarly surprises since the retags are quite hard to identify, even compared to regular retags that are already entierly hidden from surface Rust.
So I wonder, should we maybe say that these types are effectively implicitly wrapped in a `MaybeDangling`? In other words, the references captures by closures / coroutines are just forwarded entirely unchanged if the closure / coroutine itself is moved around.

(Reminder that MaybeDangling is a bad name as one major usecase is "wont actually dangle but I want to suppress retagging".)

618186989.en: Why extend ABI compatibility at all at this point? I feel like the `fn_cast!` idea is just plain better than ABI compatibility, especially the variant that abstracts over actual ABI differences and allows all mismatches that can be transmuted. And once (/if) that’s implemented and stabilized, ABI compatibility seems like a weird legacy thing we can freeze in time and otherwise ignore.
618186989.zh: Why extend ABI compatibility at all at this point? I feel like the `fn_cast!` idea is just plain better than ABI compatibility, especially the variant that abstracts over actual ABI differences and allows all mismatches that can be transmuted. And once (/if) that’s implemented and stabilized, ABI compatibility seems like a weird legacy thing we can freeze in time and otherwise ignore.

618187771.en: It makes sense to for example be allowed to define a type that C will call as `extern "C" fn(&mut T)` if it has the invariant that it will always be called with an exclusively owned pointer to reduce the amount of useless boilerplate in the body and to allow defining it as safe function. Without ABI compatibility between `&mut T` and `*mut T`this wouldn't be possible. `fn_cast!` doesn't help with that as there is no place to insert it for `#[unsafe(no_mangle)]`.

618198341.en:
The original RFC specified that the ABI should be the same https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/2195-really-tagged-unions.md#guide-level-explanation.

> An enum can currently be adorned with `#[repr(Int)]` where `Int` is one of Rust's integer types (u8, isize, etc). For C-like enums -- enums which have no variants with associated data -- this specifies that the enum should have the ABI of that integer type (size, alignment, and calling convention).

I'd have expected that to be true. That said, I don't actually know of non-FFI use cases that would care. There are plenty of FFI use cases which would, though.

618201579.en: In general, outside of backwards compatibility / churn concerns, I think it would have been better and simpler if Rust was very restrictive about ABI compatibility in the calling convention sense, to the point that there's essentially only one "correct" equivalent of any C type and function signature. Any instance of using using other types on the Rust side than the raw C equivalent would require some explicit opt-in (like `fn_cast!`) for allowing that one function to be called with a specific different signature. That would avoid placing any restrictions on CFI and Miri for finding type confusion bugs, while still allowing *explicit* mapping from C types to richer Rust types when intended and helpful.

One reason why I’d like to claw back as much ABI compatibility as possible is because anything that we keep as non-EB (because we don’t consider it sufficiently useful to CFI) can come back to haunt us later, if it later turns out to be more useful to make it EB. If we can slowly replace *all* reliance on ABI compatibility with CFI-friendly equivalents, then we won’t ever have to go through a second odyssey of telling people that code from 10 years ago, which we said was fine five years ago when we introduced EB for the sake of CFI, actually should be changed after all.

These assume that ABI compatibility in Rust is also **symmetric** (so together with transitivity, an equivalence relation). Is that a given? Transitivity seems obvious, but I don't see why it needs to be symmetric. In fact, the docs at https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.fn.html#abi-compatibility seem to contain at least one clearly asymmetric case: 
>The ABI strings are guaranteed to be compatible if they are the same, or if the caller ABI string is `$X-unwind` and the callee ABI string is `$X`, where `$X` is one of the following: ...

In the enum case, for example, it could be reasonable that you can call `fn(int)` as `fn(enum_foo)` or as `fn(enum_bar)`, but not `fn(enum_foo)` as either other type.

614944346.en:
All of this talk about atomic-`memcpy`, volatile-`memcpy`, etc. makes me think what we really need is a uber-`memcpy` where you can independently select whether the input and/or output are atomic, volatile, aligned, potentially-overlapping, really a `memset`, etc.

The idea is we propose adding it to LLVM and then it becomes the replacement for `llvm.memcpy`, `llvm.memcpy.element.unordered.atomic`, etc. (though probably with some kind of migration strategy). Because the flags are independently set for the input and output, that prevents problems where both input and output are atomic/volatile so the compiler generates a extra load when all you want is volatile/atomic store, or an extra store when all you want is volatile/atomic store. 614944346.zh:
All of this talk about atomic-`memcpy`, volatile-`memcpy`, etc. makes me think what we really need is a uber-`memcpy` where you can independently select whether the input and/or output are atomic, volatile, aligned, potentially-overlapping, really a `memset`, etc.

The idea is we propose adding it to LLVM and then it becomes the replacement for `llvm.memcpy`, `llvm.memcpy.element.unordered.atomic`, etc. (though probably with some kind of migration strategy). Because the flags are independently set for the input and output, that prevents problems where both input and output are atomic/volatile so the compiler generates a extra load when all you want is volatile/atomic store, or an extra store when all you want is volatile/atomic store. Being both volatile and atomic allows you to have volatile ops that interact with fences and other atomics.

614939545.en:
I have several questions/thoughts about how memory accesses interact with signal handlers. (In particular, with async-signal-safe signal handlers that might still access Rust-allocated memory, such as atomics in `static`s... and presumably local variables within a signal handler implemented in Rust are also affected, under a literal reading of documentation.)

# Spurious signals

First, if the signal handler is treated as not semantically guaranteed to be called at the expected time, I *think* we can use inline-asm-style storytelling, even on the current version of rust before https://github.com/rust-lang/unsafe-code-guidelines/issues/610 lands.

In particular, say that some read or write, A, triggers a signal B that causes signal handler C to run. We could tell the story that "signal B can be spuriously raised at any time, and A is not responsible for that". To maintain that story, we can no longer assume that C runs iff A starts to execute, but at least -- as far as I know -- this would make running C sound.

(So long as nothing tries to detect that signal B was in fact caused by memory access A and make some unchecked assumption based on that fact. Nothing in the language itself or in `std` ought to do that, and at *worst* some other crate could go out of its way to include code which is inconsistent with this story, perhaps installing a signal handler and deciding whether to execute UB based on the contents of a `siginfo_t`.)

I don't think this even requires volatile accesses. Any sort of memory access should work.

The cost is that if you try to use this somewhat-simplistic story to justify a segfaulting read (for instance), then you have to accept the possibility of a segfault occurring at any time whatsoever.

It's more useful for memory-mapped files and SIGBUS. We could slightly refine the story to "spurious SIGBUSes can occur during any time that any memory-mapped file is shorter than its mapping". Any operation which changes the length of a file or a mapping (whether from the current process or an external process), which already has externally-observable side effects, can be said to also manage the flag permitting these spurious SIGBUSes. Under this story, reads and writes to shared memory-mapped files are not unsound in the face of external processes being able to truncate files, even if there's a registered SIGBUS handler that accesses Rust-allocated memory and may or may not abort the process (though, realistically, a SIGBUS handler should abort the process). Instead, if such a truncation occurs, the result is well-defined... if less than ideal for the victim process.

Under this story, do the memory accesses to memory-mapped files even need to be volatile? (...separately, there's still the concern of data races, and absent mixed-size atomic accesses, I suppose that volatile reads and writes are the best option.)

(Edge case: maybe the program is statically linked to the responsible OS code, and that code somehow avoids executing an operation which is considered externally observable. Then there could be a problem. This argument requires there to be *something* external to the AM that could hypothetically be tracking the lengths of memory-mapped files and their mappings, and could hypothetically send SIGBUSes based on that state.)

# Guaranteed signals

Once volatile accesses are permitted to trap... can a signal handler access Rust-allocated memory and then abort the process, while still being guaranteed to be called when the access occurs? Or, as in the above scenario, can it not be guaranteed that a custom signal handler would run at the expected time?

I'm trying to think of hypothetical transformations that would break this guarantee, but if the custom signal handler is only reading and writing atomics (and its own local variables), then transformations that break the signal handler would also break any other thread looking at the atomics at the wrong time. (Even if this all occurs moments before the process is terminated.) Thread-local state could hypothetically be clobbered and un-clobbered before and after a volatile operation without breaking other threads, but since signal handlers ought to be treated as running in a different thread, that shouldn't break a sound signal handler.

Note that `std`, on some platforms, [registers a signal handler](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/b070f45ad92ed45b20e57d9483a21657d0d00715/library/std/src/sys/pal/unix/stack_overflow.rs) implemented in Rust for SIGBUS and SIGSEGV on some platforms. (Its job is to check if the SIGBUS or SIGSEGV looks like it was caused by a stack overflow, and if so, print a nicer error message and abort the process.) Since that signal handler has local variables in Rust allocations, a literal reading of
> The access is allowed to trap. It can also cause other side-effects, but those must not affect Rust-allocated memory in any way.

indicates that volatile operations are not permitted to result in a SIGBUS or SIGSEGV on those platforms (unless those signal handlers are unregistered first), which doesn't seem intended.

Story code can go where FFI calls are as well, right? Assuming that *some* FFI is involved any time a memory mapping is created (or has its length change) or a file's length changes, you can say that such FFI reports the changes to that background thread. That background thread records the data, and whenever it determines that there is a memory-mapped file shorter than its mapping, it may choose to send SIGBUSes to the thread with the overlong mapping (up until the background thread sees that there is no longer a memory-mapped file shorter than its mapping in that thread, based on the supposed reports from the mmap and file FFI calls).

Any SIGBUSes received from performing memory accesses on a memory mapping whose backing file is too short, even if Rust/LLVM reorder, hoist them, or do whatever else, should be a subset of the SIGBUSes that could have been sent by that background thread (...ignoring fine details like the contents of the signal's `siginfo_t`. Maybe we can pretend that the background thread has some magic OS permissions that let it forge whatever signal it wants; should be equally sound as far as the language is concerned.). Therefore, the actual FFI code refines this story.
