@_**Quy Nguyen|303115** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/136281-t-lang.2Fwg-unsafe-code-guidelines/topic/Weak.20provenance.20function.20pointers/near/278230988):
```quote
On non-CHERI architectures, does function pointer provenance mean anything to the optimizer/is it used for optimizations? It seems like it should be really easy to spec out something for them, as you don't have to deal with one-past-the-end or Stacked Borrows.
```
lccc's model has limited provenance in function pointers.
`[ptr.root]#5` says that every root pointer (other than null pointers) - a "source" of provenance for valid pointers - is a pointer to one of 4 things, and it lists "function" as one of them. Two things this allows are:
* not being able to take a pointer to something else (say, a target/label), cast it to a function and call it (even if they happen end up at same address - which is completely reasonable for a target to do, if it's the first target in the function and prolouge elision occurs). This is exploited by <https://github.com/LightningCreations/lccc/blob/main/xlang/xlang_backend/src/lib.rs#L1404> to avoid computing an address unnecessarily.
* Being able to assume certain functions that are unreachable aren't called from outside their declaring module (and thus, if not called within that module, not called at all).

613555516.en:
So, there's an interesting implication, that just came up on the Community Discord.
If functions can be deduplicated such that pointers to different functions compare equal: Return values of functions can have different provenance, even if they have equal bytewise values in all cases (they both might return a reference to a string literal/promoted constant, that happens to compare equal in the common length prefix, but have different total sizes). Thus, such function pointers to the different functions will need to be distinguished, to have results that differ in their results at runtime.
In the case where two equivalent-value returning functions yield values that differ in provenance, this means that function pointers do need to have provenance themselves (or they cannot be so deduplicated).

613699496.en:
@_**RalfJ|120791** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/136281-t-opsem/topic/Weak.20provenance.20function.20pointers/near/613634477):
````quote
where in the pipeline does merging happen?
if there's a merge pass on machine IR then it could easily happen that functions with different UB get merged
````

I'm pretty sure there is merging at *some* stage in the backend but I don't think when merging is done or pass ordering matters to what I was thinking.

Since we generally require each pass in isolation to refine the UB (i.e., only remove non-det and UB), overall the pipeline should monotonically make the program more refined. I concluded from this that "merge two functions that have different UB" does not seem like a valid pass -- you can only refine the functions until they don't have different UB, *then* merge them, and afterwards you're committed to them being the same function and not having different UB any more. Even this property is nontrivial due to the "IPO and Derefinement" class of issues, but these are compiler bugs, not painful consequences of opsem non-determinism.

Your example in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/160202 shows I missed something in this reasoning. Each of the three optimization steps you list is a valid refinement. I think the key step there that I didn't consider is that a call via function pointer can be devirtualized and inlined without ever making any decision about the fn pointer equality, so the equality check can stick around until runtime while the call didn't. I don't think LLVM will realistically *introduce* code that is susceptible to this, but unfortunately the `fn_ptr_eq` docs encourage writing code that looks scarily close to your abstract example.

613733085.en: it seems like, in practice, LLVM is optimizing the fn ptr comparison to false in a modified example from #160202, because it believes that the call would be UB if the functions were equal.  In fact it even creates an `assume` that the pointers are not equal, because it believes that the call is UB.  This is at the very least an incredibly suspicious step because the docs claim "if the pointers are equal, you're good" and LLVM is thinking "if the pointers are equal, it's very bad".

613455256.en:
I realized that Miri does not do a proper typed loan when a reference `r` is used e.g. in `&raw const (*r).field`. MiniRust naturally does the right checks there since everything goes via typed loads, but Miri only does validity checks on typed copies and otherwise relies on the operation consuming a value to check its validity -- which we do most of the time, but not when dereferencing a reference. https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/160012 fixes that.
Now I wonder, are there other operations on references that I missed where we also need to do these checks? I thought casts may be a problem, but I added tests and they are fine. it looks like implicit deref's get added there during MIR building or so. Though now that I spell this out, this means custom MIR that avoids the implicit casts would not be checked properly, and more importantly we wouldn't represent the actual MIR semantics, so I may have to revisit that...

Are there other operations I missed, built-in language operations that use a reference and should check its validity?
This also applies to raw pointers that may have an invalid vtable.

611847263.en: For LLVM's special allocator treatment, we need some place to insert the new intrinsics @**Nikita Popov** is [proposing](https://discourse.llvm.org/t/rfc-allocator-provenance-model/91106). So if we make this a mere trait, then it becomes a safety requirement for people implementing the trait that they must add those intrinsics to their impl. A wrapper type has the advantage that we can just add the intrinsics ourselves without having to publicly expose them. (We'll also have to somehow magically add them when users set the `#[global_allocator]`, i.e. we'll need to somewhere have wrapper functions rather than directly invoking the user's methods.)
611847263.zh: For LLVM's special allocator treatment, we need some place to insert the new intrinsics @**Nikita Popov** is [proposing](https://discourse.llvm.org/t/rfc-allocator-provenance-model/91106). So if we make this a mere trait, then it becomes a safety requirement for people implementing the trait that they must add those intrinsics to their impl. A wrapper type has the advantage that we can just add the intrinsics ourselves without having to publicly expose them. (We'll also have to somehow magically add them when users set the `#[global_allocator]`, i.e. we'll need to somewhere have wrapper functions rather than directly invoking the user's methods.)

611848267.en:
`noalias` could in principle be independent of LLVM's special allocator treatment, but I see no good reason to separate the two.
Also putting `noalias` on `Box` funnily becomes *less* problematic if the allocator gets special treatment: the special treatment makes it so that the `dealloc` method receives a pointer with the original provenance that was returned from `alloc`, so even if `dealloc` gets inlined the compiler can *not* make use of any `noalias` that was put on the pointer *before* it was passed to `dealloc`. IOW, having the special semantics solves https://github.com/rust-lang/miri/issues/2104.

611854976.en:
@_**RalfJ|120791** [said](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/136281-t-opsem/topic/Enabling.20compiler.20magic.20on.20custom.20allocators/near/611847263):
```quote
For LLVM's special allocator treatment, we need some place to insert the new intrinsics @**Nikita Popov** is [proposing](https://discourse.llvm.org/t/rfc-allocator-provenance-model/91106). So if we make this a mere trait, then it becomes a safety requirement for people implementing the trait that they must add those intrinsics to their impl. A wrapper type has the advantage that we can just add the intrinsics ourselves without having to publicly expose them. (We'll also have to somehow magically add them when users set the `#[global_allocator]`, i.e. we'll need to somewhere have wrapper functions rather than directly invoking the user's methods.)
```

Is it actually a safety requirement that allocator implementations use those intrinsics? Allocators should work just fine without using them, which would make them optional. I would just leave it to the allocator's discretion whether to use these or not.
